title: Why Belgrade's new government should not let the Vertical Gas Corridor slip
gist: After the Student List won 52.6% and ended Progressive Party rule, the author (Olivier Van Pelt per the text) argues Serbia's new government must keep its September commitment to the Vertical Gas Corridor, whose western branch via North Macedonia (~1.5 bcm/yr by 2028) plus the Bulgaria interconnector could cover Serbia's 2.7 bcm demand from non-Russian sources. The corridor is framed as aligning with the Student List's transparency, growth and private-investment platform without forcing a Brussels-vs-Moscow choice.

themes.theme: Serbia's political transition and ambiguous EU/Russia stance

insights.claim: Serbia's Student List won 52.6 percent of the vote and an outright parliamentary majority in the October 25, 2026 early election, ending fourteen years of Serbian Progressive Party rule after President Aleksandar Vučić resigned on September 27, 2026.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Regime change in Serbia reopens energy, sanctions and EU-accession policy — a key Balkan geopolitical variable.

insights.claim: Student List representatives send mixed signals: some told Russian media they are content with the existing Moscow–Belgrade gas arrangement and do not envisage sanctions on Russia, while Ilija Srdanović stressed shared European values and the EU path.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Policy direction is unresolved; expect continued hedging rather than sharp realignment, so price in slow-moving change on Russia sanctions.

insights.claim: Gazprom supplies Serbia roughly 2.2 bcm of natural gas a year at below-market rates.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Below-market Russian gas is a strong incentive against diversification; switching to competitive supply may raise near-term costs.

insights.claim: NIS, Serbia's only oil refinery and majority-owned by Gazprom Neft, has been under US sanctions since January 2025, with crude flowing on US waivers while its sale to Hungary's MOL is pending.

themes.theme: Vertical Gas Corridor as a diversification route

insights.claim: The Vertical Gas Corridor carries Greek LNG and Azerbaijani gas from the Trans Adriatic Pipeline north through Bulgaria and Romania to Moldova and Ukraine.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Growing south-to-north gas route benefits Greek LNG terminals, TAP and Azeri supply as substitutes for Russian gas in the region.
insights.locator: The Vertical Gas Corridor offers a way out.

insights.claim: The expanded western branch connecting Serbia via North Macedonia would add around 1.5 bcm a year of import capacity on completion in 2028; with the existing Bulgaria-Serbia interconnector, Serbia could meet its 2.7 bcm annual demand from non-Russian sources.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: By 2028 Serbia could theoretically fully replace Russian gas — a structural loss for Gazprom's Balkan market if executed.
insights.quote: Serbia would have the capacity to satisfy its 2.7 bcm a year gas demand from non-Russian sources
insights.locator: The Vertical Gas Corridor offers a way out.

insights.claim: State-owned Srbijagas will build the €153 million Serbian section of the new corridor link.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Tender process for the €153m section is a near-term test of procurement reforms and a contracting opportunity.
insights.quote: State-owned Srbijagas will build the €153 million Serbian section of the new link

insights.claim: Competing gas suppliers would put downward pressure on prices, weaken the case for price caps, and open room for private capital in Serbian infrastructure, making the corridor a catalyst for private-sector involvement.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Liberalization path for Serbian energy markets could unlock private investment beyond gas.

themes.theme: Aligning the corridor with the Student Plan

insights.claim: The author argues the Vertical Gas Corridor matches the Student List's 'Student Plan' pillars — contract transparency, an innovation-based high-value economy, and ending import-lobby dominance — letting the government act without choosing between Brussels and Moscow.
insights.speaker: srothbardt
insights.so_what: Framing diversification as anticorruption rather than geopolitics raises odds it survives the transition.
